PullRequest.Title: chat: bridge host-owned Microsoft credentials to Copilot
PullRequest.Body:

* Read our Pull Request guidelines:
  https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests
* Associate an issue with the Pull Request.

Builds on merged #345132 and targets `main`. This is the credential-bridge layer of native [stack #345731](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/stack/345731): it lets the Agent Host's Copilot provider use Microsoft credentials that VS Code owns, without adding a sign-in flow, a protocol method or a token store.

## What this changes

- **Host bridge.** When `chat.agentHost.copilot.m365.enabled` was on at the time the host started (the startup-effective value from #345132), the Copilot provider passes the SDK's `entra.tokenProvider` a callback backed by credentials received over the existing `authenticate` request. `CopilotClient`, `RuntimeConnection.forStdio` and the separate runtime process are unchanged. The callback never waits: it returns a matching stored credential, or `unavailable` while advertising the requirement through the existing `auth/required` notification. A later delivery satisfies a later retry.
- **Binding.** A credential is accepted only for the advertised resource and scopes, from the Microsoft account the host is already bound to. A different account is rejected rather than substituted. Exchange, derived credentials and enforcement stay in the runtime.
- **Optional alternatives.** With the setting on, the GitHub Copilot resource and the Entra resources are advertised with `required: false`, so neither sign-in is a prerequisite for the other. This is metadata only: an operation still needs its own credential and fails with an auth-required error without it. With the setting off, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise declarations and enforcement are unchanged. An outstanding Microsoft requirement does not affect automation readiness, which depends on the GitHub credential as on `main`. The provider publishes one outstanding requirement at a time and GitHub's takes priority, so a pending Microsoft requirement cannot hide a GitHub challenge; a Microsoft requirement raised meanwhile is published once the GitHub one clears.
- **Generic resolver fix.** The client resolver treated `getSessions(undefined)` results as token-bearing. The Microsoft provider returns account placeholders with no scopes for that call, so a default Microsoft account never produced a usable token. The resolver now selects the account, then requests the advertised scopes from the advertised authorization server for that account, and checks the returned account and scopes before forwarding. If that scoped request fails, the remaining authorization servers are tried, and the provider's error is rethrown if none resolves the resource; it then stops the rest of that pass, as any error from the resolver does. This applies to any protected resource; there is no Copilot-specific classification.
- **Recovery.** Retry and prompt sequencing for an `auth/required` notification matches `main`: the client re-sends its current token once, then tries another signed-in session, then opens the existing sign-in dialog when the same token is challenged again. One addition: the dialog is skipped when the challenged credential's provider is not the one the dialog signs in (`IDefaultAccountService.getDefaultAccountAuthenticationProvider()`). A Microsoft resource therefore never opens the GitHub sign-in dialog and stays silent until a replacement token is available. The same applies to any other provider the dialog does not sign in, where `main` opens a dialog that cannot supply the credential. An earlier revision of this PR treated every `expired` challenge as a rejected token and never re-sent it. That is reverted, because the host also sends `expired` when its credential was merely cleared by another client, and it expects a re-send.
- **Lifetime.** Microsoft credentials follow the same lifecycle as GitHub credentials in the host. Authority is established when the host accepts a credential for an advertised requirement. Accepted, unexpired credentials survive the last client disconnecting; a disconnect is not a sign-out. Any connected client can withdraw them. The host then advertises the missing credential so a client that is still signed in can re-supply it, and requests the same deferred runtime restart as a cleared GitHub token, so running turns finish first. A delivery or withdrawal still in flight when its transport closes is processed. Stored credentials replayed to the provider are re-validated against the bound account and the advertised resource and scopes. An earlier revision tied withdrawal and delivery to the connection that supplied the credentials and stopped the runtime immediately; that is removed on purpose so the two providers behave the same, and hardening that applies to both is left for separate work. Credentials are held in memory only.

No new protocol method, RPC, setting, policy, persistent credential store or dependency change is introduced.

## Not included

- Service discovery, selected-service activation, conversation binding, account UI, model picker and usage are separate layers above this one.
- This layer has no native Microsoft sign-in entry point. The existing setup flow's "Microsoft" option is GitHub sign-in through a Microsoft identity, not Entra resource acquisition.

## Known open items

- Two review threads are intentionally left open as valid and not addressed here: a session removal that arrives while a push for a different account is in flight is matched only against the pending delivery ([thread](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/345730#discussion_r4530624028)), and the host remembers only the most recently challenged token per resource ([thread](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/345730#discussion_r4530623945)).
- After the explicit sign-in prompt, work is cancelled only if the default account signed out or its provider changed. A session replaced by sign-in under the same provider is forwarded; this is not a check that it belongs to the same account. The host's account binding is unchanged and is what rejects a different Microsoft account.
- When the runtime rejects a Microsoft token and no replacement exists yet, the client's re-send is refused by the host and logged as a failed authentication. A re-send is recorded only after it succeeds, so this can repeat on later challenges until the provider returns a different token. This is read from the code and is not covered by a test.
- Because withdrawal follows GitHub, signing out no longer interrupts a running turn, another signed-in client can re-supply a credential after a withdrawal, and a withdrawal that arrives late can clear an identity another client just supplied. These are accepted for now.
- Replay does not bind an account by itself. The Microsoft identity requirement is advertised only after the runtime asks for it, and the account is bound when an accepted delivery is stored. A resource credential whose requirement is already satisfied is no longer advertised, so replaying it is rejected and it stays in the store unchanged.

## Reading the commits

The branch was rebased onto newer `main`; one conflict was resolved, in a test import. Some intermediate designs are removed by later commits (a private host capability, a shared/client split of protected resources, a rewrite of challenge recovery, and connection-scoped ownership of Microsoft credentials), so the final diff is easier to review than each commit in turn. The commits that carry the final design:

- `1855ca15c14` host bridge
- `2acb1c03e21` accepted credentials survive disconnects
- `ae9ad781deb` generic scoped acquisition, private capability removed
- `72c17c13c7d` rejected-session history kept by token fingerprint
- `1d36e99e3f5` optional alternatives
- `2e56d60b55a` explicit re-sign-in and scope-less removal fixes
- `97fd0a88601` challenge recovery sequencing restored to match `main`, with the provider check
- `1c0012a646e` Microsoft credential lifetime aligned with GitHub
- `71c8f3cd424` three review fixes: GitHub requirement published first, real sessions kept for a resource without scopes, account-scoped lookup failure handled
- `f6103caeb02` correction to the third of those: the lookup failure is rethrown when no other authorization server resolves the resource, instead of being reported as an unavailable provider
- `d820e183217` and `cf77a71301c` contributor notes

## Validation

Local runs are on Windows. Counts are per invocation and overlap; they are not a unique total.

On the current head `f6103caeb02` the workflows had not finished when this was written.

Manual smoke check at the earlier head `71c8f3cd424`, in an isolated development build with the declared SDK `1.0.31-preview.1` and bundled runtime `1.0.109-1` installed. With the setting off, and again in a separate fresh host with the setting on: startup signed in to GitHub from a saved isolated profile, the host accepted the GitHub credentials, a separate runtime process started, and one tool-free chat request returned exactly the expected fixed reply and completed once. No Microsoft credential was supplied. The same check also passed at the earlier heads `1c0012a646e` and `cf77a71301c`. It was not repeated at `f6103caeb02`, which changes only how a failed lookup is handled.

## Limits of this validation

- The smoke check covers healthy GitHub setup and one request only. No challenge, withdrawal, sign-out or replay was staged and no Microsoft credential was involved, so neither the recovery sequence, the Microsoft credential lifetime change, nor the cases fixed in `71c8f3cd424` and `f6103caeb02` were exercised against a real host with real credentials. They are covered by unit tests with fake authentication providers and hosts, and the lifetime change also by the transport test with synthetic credentials.
- The Microsoft path is covered by controlled authentication-provider fixtures and by the transport test with synthetic credentials. A real Microsoft sign-in and Entra token acquisition through this layer were not exercised, nor were entitlement or inference.
- Tests that inject a Microsoft default account are generic coverage of the resolver. The product's default account remains GitHub or GitHub Enterprise.
- Full repository suites were not run locally; the host tests above are a focused selection.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent host startup with the Microsoft credential bridge enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: CopilotAgent eagerly creates a lightweight in-memory bridge and passes a synchronous tokenProvider into SDK client creation. Runtime startup does not wait for credential acquisition: a cache miss returns unavailable immediately and publishes a requirement asynchronously.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish changed protected-resource metadata/auth-required state from agent host to workbench and later deliver authenticate back to the host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one publication per distinct resource/reason/scope state because requireCredential deduplicates identical requirements; Microsoft has one discovery resource and two mapped token resources.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No Microsoft requirement or credential IPC existed; GitHub authentication already used the host/workbench authentication channel.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The SDK callback returns unavailable synchronously, so publication and credential delivery are off the immediate callback critical path; a later authenticated operation may retry after delivery.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Activate an authentication provider and enumerate existing sessions, optionally acquire scopes for the selected account
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Serial per advertised resource and authorization server; for account-placeholder providers, one account enumeration plus one scoped query for the preferred account. The bridge advertises only the currently required Microsoft resource.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Existing resources performed provider activation/session enumeration; the diff adds one scoped account query only when account enumeration does not itself contain a usable scoped credential.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before the workbench can deliver a credential, but not before the host token callback returns unavailable. Remote initial handshake skips required:false resources.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of agents, distinct protected resources, authorization servers, and signed-in sessions. Microsoft additions are statically bounded to one discovery resource plus two known audience resources, and duplicate requirement states are coalesced.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Protected resources and authorization servers are processed serially in the workbench resolver; identical authenticate RPCs share a pending promise per key. No new concurrency burst is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Host credentials are keyed by resource/scopes and expiry; workbench forwarding deduplicates completed and pending credentials. Missing Microsoft credentials are represented by a deduplicated observable requirement rather than a negative token cache; repeat identical SDK requests do not republish state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: constructor, token callback, observable publication, resolver, and authenticate RPC paths were traced directly.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Authentication provider implementations may perform keychain or refresh work internally, but cardinality is bounded and the new query is conditional on account-only enumeration.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The eager object is lightweight, misses do not block the SDK callback, and expensive provider work is bounded and deduplicated.

Scenarios.Scenario: Runtime requests a Microsoft audience token during login or an M365-backed operation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The synchronous SDK tokenProvider checks the in-memory credential store. A hit returns immediately; a miss invalidates an expired/rejected entry when necessary, publishes one requirement, and returns unavailable. Workbench session resolution and authenticate IPC happen before a later retry can succeed, not within the callback.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Authenticate request carrying the selected scoped session token and account metadata
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One RPC per changed resource/scope/token key; concurrent identical forwarding shares one pending promise and completed values suppress repeats.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: There was no Microsoft token delivery; existing GitHub resources used the same deduplicated authentication RPC cache.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for a later successful token retry, but a missing token request itself finishes immediately as unavailable.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One provider lookup and normally one session query for a required resource; account-placeholder enumeration can add one scoped query. Multiple authorization servers are tried serially.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The resolver previously selected already-enumerated sessions; the conditional account-scoped query is new and necessary to turn an account placeholder into the advertised scoped credential.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On the asynchronous credential-supply path; it can delay a successful retry but does not block the initial token callback.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct Microsoft audiences/scopes requested by the packaged runtime. Audience validation restricts requests to two static mappings, and one requirement replaces the prior requirement for the same resource.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: SDK callback work is synchronous. Workbench lookup is serial per resolver invocation; recovery coalesces concurrent challenges by protected-resource key.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Warm valid credentials are returned from AgentHostAuthenticationService. Expired or skip-cache requests invalidate that resource and remember only the most recently rejected host token; workbench forwarding coalesces pending requests and caches the last credential key.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: request validation, cache reads, challenge state, requirement deduplication, and workbench pending-recovery maps were inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual provider token refresh latency is implementation-dependent, but no collection-driven or unbounded fan-out was introduced.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Boundary work is one-per-changed credential, coalesced, and bounded to known audiences.

Scenarios.Scenario: Microsoft sign-out or rejected/expired credential recovery
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Sign-out clears authority and the bounded mapped resources, publishes a single discovery requirement, then schedules a runtime restart after active shared-runtime turns finish. Expired/rejected token requests synchronously invalidate only the affected resource before returning unavailable.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish token removals and the replacement authentication requirement; receive replacement authenticate
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: A sign-out scans the authentication store once for each of three static resources and emits per matching stored credential; replacement delivery is deduplicated per resource/scope/token.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Microsoft state and restart behavior did not exist; analogous GitHub credential clearing already restarted runtime state.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runtime restart is intentionally deferred until running turns finish; credential replacement is required for future Microsoft-backed operations.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Stop and later recreate the shared Copilot runtime after authority revocation
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One requested restart per effective revocation while authority exists; repeated empty-token revocations return early once authority is cleared.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Microsoft revocation could not trigger a restart because no bridge existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the active-turn critical path because restart waits for running shared-runtime turns to finish; later sessions may pay cold restart cost.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Stored credential keys for three statically known resources and number of active turns. Repeated revocations without authority are no-ops.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Resource invalidation is synchronous and serial over small maps. Runtime restart requests use the existing restart coordination and wait for active turns rather than spawning concurrent runtimes.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Revocation clears authority, challenges, requirements, and all stored tokens for the static resources. Replacement requirements are deduplicated. The workbench rejection cache is connection-scoped and cleared on session removal or connection reset.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: revocation, invalidation loops, observable update, and restart callback were traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Cold runtime restart duration varies, but it is tied to explicit sign-out and not repeated by duplicate empty revocations.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Cleanup and restart have bounded cardinality and preserve active-turn scheduling.

Scenarios.Scenario: Authentication-session changes and remote connection bootstrap
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Session changes reconcile removed credentials, then re-run protected-resource authentication. Remote bootstrap resolves only resources marked required; with the bridge enabled, GitHub and Microsoft alternatives are optional, so they are excluded from the initial remote handshake.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve provider IDs and enumerate sessions for each applicable protected resource
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Serial per agent/resource, with duplicate token sends suppressed by AgentHostAuthTokenCache. Removed-session reconciliation deduplicates resources with a local set.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Full protected-resource reconciliation on root/session changes already existed; the diff changes account selection and adds conditional scoped acquisition.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs before authentication-pending clears for local/remote contributions; remote bootstrap does not query optional Microsoft resources.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Remote connection authenticate RPC for a changed selected session
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one changed-token RPC per resource/scope key; warm identical credentials are suppressed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Remote connections already forwarded required protected-resource credentials over IPC.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Part of connection authentication settling only for required advertised resources; optional alternatives are skipped by the initial resolver.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Connected remote hosts, agents, resources, and removed sessions. Reconciliation remains serial per connection; resources are deduplicated during removal handling and token RPCs are cached per connection.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Connections may authenticate independently, while resources within a connection are serial. Existing per-key pending promises prevent duplicate sends within a connection.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Each connection owns a cache dropped on connection disposal. Completed and pending tokens coalesce repeats; generation invalidation cancels stale forwards. Remote initial resolver ignores required:false resources.
